title: A Kitchen Rooflight Works Best Where the Daylight Is Missing
seo: Kitchen Extension Rooflight Ideas: Light, Layout and Shade
description: Explore kitchen extension rooflight ideas, from narrow roof glazing to light above a dining table, with practical advice on layout, shading and cleaning.
deck: The brightest patch in the photograph is only part of the story. Start with the room that needs the light.
alt: Long rectangular rooflight above an oak worktop in a narrow kitchen extension with a garden door
inline_sources: Rectangular rooflight in a deep ceiling reveal above a small oak dining table
Close view of a rooflight reveal with a partially drawn fitted pleated shade
body:
A kitchen-extension rooflight is most useful when it brings daylight to a part of the plan that the garden windows cannot reach. That might be the old rear room, a worktop beside a boundary wall or a dining table in the middle of the house. Choose its position alongside the kitchen layout, then plan the glass, shade, ventilation and cleaning access as one job.

Rear extensions have a familiar blind spot. The new room beside the garden looks lovely, while the room you walked through to get there has become a little gloomy. A bigger set of doors at the back does not always fix it. Sometimes the useful move is to put daylight further into the plan.

The short answer

Put the opening where it earns its place

Mark the darkest useful area on the floor plan before drawing a rooflight. Compare a narrow strip beside the kitchen, a compact opening over the table and glazing near the junction of old and new rooms. Check the roof structure and the sun's path, and include shading and maintenance in the brief.

Find the part of the kitchen that needs daylight

Walk through the existing house on an ordinary cloudy day. Where do you turn on a light first? Is the problem the sink, the route through the room or the old dining area that the extension will sit beyond? Those are different problems, and they may need different openings.

Draw the extension together with the rooms behind it. A rooflight positioned near the original rear wall can help the connection between old and new feel less abrupt, but a beam, deep ceiling or tall cupboard may interrupt the light. Ask the designer to show a section through this junction. A plan tells you where the glass sits; the section explains what lies between the glass and the room.

Also mark the places where strong light would be unwelcome. A screen used for work, a glossy counter or the chair facing the afternoon sun deserves attention before the opening is fixed. Good daylight should make the room easier to use.

Three rooflight layouts worth considering

A narrow strip beside the kitchen

A long opening can bring light along the depth of a narrow extension. Visually, it can separate a solid wall from the ceiling and make a modest room feel less hemmed in. Keep the relationship to cabinets deliberate. A strip that stops awkwardly above one cupboard can look like the kitchen and roof were designed on different days.

A compact rooflight above the table

This gives the dining area a clear centre without needing an elaborate ceiling. Check the table in its everyday position, including the space for chairs to move. If you regularly shift the furniture, a slightly less exact alignment may suit the room better than a composition that only works for one photograph.

Glazing near the old rear wall

This is worth exploring when the middle room is the weak point. The opening needs to work with the structure at the former external wall and the ceiling levels on either side. It is a design conversation to have early, while the extension's shape can still change.

The reveal matters as much as the rectangle of glass

A rooflight is seen through the thickness of the roof. The depth, angle and finish of that opening affect how it feels from below. A deep shaft can frame a beautiful patch of sky, but it can also conceal much of the glass when viewed from the adjoining room.

Ask to see the opening from the places where you will spend time: at the sink, seated at the table and entering from the hall. A perspective taken directly beneath the glass gives you very little information about those everyday views.

Keep ceiling fittings on the same drawing. Pendant lights, extraction, downlights and blind housings all need space. If the rooflight is above the dining table, the pendant does not automatically belong directly under it. A wall light or a pendant moved to another part of the room may leave the sky view clearer.

Choose shade before the first hot afternoon

Daylight and summer comfort need to be considered together. The orientation, amount of glass, surrounding shade and the rest of the extension all affect the result. Ask the designer or glazing supplier to explain the proposed solar-control specification in the context of your room, rather than choosing glass from a single headline figure.

Check which shading products fit the exact rooflight, how they are operated and where the controls will go. The VELUX flat-glass rooflight product sheet, for example, describes compatible anti-heat and blackout options. That is a reminder to specify the complete system; it is not a claim that every blind fits every opening.

An opening rooflight may form part of a ventilation strategy, but it does not replace a properly planned kitchen extraction system. Think about rain, security and what happens when nobody is home to operate it. If it is powered, arrange the wiring and controls before the ceiling is finished.

Leave enough solid ceiling for the room to settle

There is no rule that a successful extension needs the largest possible glazed roof. Solid areas provide places for insulation, services and lighting, and can give the room a more sheltered atmosphere. A modest opening in the right position can be a more satisfying feature than glass spread across the entire ceiling.

Relate the rooflight to the room's other openings. A large garden door already makes a strong visual statement. The roof glazing might work better as a quieter source of light further back. Keep the material palette simple enough for the moving daylight to be noticed.

If the roof cannot reasonably be altered, compare high wall glazing where the site allows it. Our clerestory window guide looks at daylight above eye level. For a hall beside a bright room, an internal window is another conversation, with a different scope of work.

Ask how it will be installed, cleaned and repaired

Before ordering, have the roof structure, waterproofing, insulation and surrounding construction designed for the chosen unit. Installation requirements vary. A dimension or roof pitch from one product sheet should not be transferred to a different rooflight because the photographs look similar.

Cleaning is easy to forget when the view is all sky. Establish how both sides of the glazing can be reached safely, who will do the work and whether the outside needs specialist access. In the VELUX sheet linked above, exterior access is required to clean the top unit. Check your proposed product just as carefully.

Ask for the full scope in the quotation: the unit, installation, weathering details, interior finishing, controls and any shading. A low price for the glass itself tells you little about the completed room. Keep the specification and maintenance information somewhere you can find them after the builders leave.

Kitchen rooflight questions

Where should a rooflight go in a kitchen extension?

Start with the area that lacks useful daylight, then coordinate the opening with the structure, worktops, table and sun exposure. The centre of the roof is not automatically the best position.

Is a rooflight over a dining table a good idea?

It can give the table a pleasing focus. Check glare, summer shade, evening lighting and whether the furniture is likely to move.

Do kitchen rooflights need blinds?

That depends on the glazing, orientation and room. Consider compatible shading during design so that a later fitting does not become an awkward compromise.

Sources and image note

title: The Pocket Door Gives a Small Room Its Corner Back
seo: Pocket Doors for Small Rooms: Layout Ideas and Trade-Offs
description: Are pocket doors right for a small room? Explore layout ideas, wall-space checks, handles, privacy and the details to resolve before choosing a system.
deck: Losing the swing of a door can help a tight plan. The wall it slides into needs just as much thought.
alt: Partly open oak pocket door connecting a compact living room to a warm plaster hallway
inline_sources: Two oak pocket door leaves partly retracted beside a dining-room opening
Recessed pull in a partly open grey pocket door above an oak floor
body:
Pocket doors can help a small room when a hinged door's swing gets in the way of furniture or circulation. The leaf slides into a cavity in the wall, leaving the opening clear. The trade-off is that the wall needs enough suitable space for the pocket, and the chosen system must meet the room's needs for privacy, access and everyday use.

You know the corner: a chair would fit there, except the door opens into it. The cupboard works, except you have to close one door before opening the other. These small collisions are where a pocket door can be useful. Its appeal is less about a dramatic disappearing panel than the ordinary convenience of getting through the room.

The short answer

Check the wall before choosing the door

Draw the opening and the full pocket on the plan. Check structure, services, wall thickness and the finished clear passage. Then try the handle, closing action and privacy arrangement in person. Specify access for maintenance before the wall is closed.

Start with the door swing you want to remove

Draw the existing door fully open, then add the furniture as it is actually used. Include a chair pulled back, a cupboard door open and someone carrying laundry. It becomes much easier to tell whether removing the swing would solve a recurring annoyance or simply make a drawing look tidier.

A single pocket door can help at a compact study, pantry or living room. A pair can connect two rooms more generously when open, then allow them to be separated. Consider how often you will close them. A heavy pair that stays open all year may be an expensive way to frame a passage.

Do not assume the opening itself will feel wider. The useful clear width depends on the complete installation, including how far the leaf retracts and the hardware. Compare the finished passage with the route you need for people and furniture.

The door disappears into a real piece of wall

The pocket occupies space beside the doorway. That length of wall must accommodate the chosen system, and it needs to be assessed for structure and concealed services before work begins. A neat photograph of a finished doorway does not show the pipes, sockets or supports that may complicate yours.

Ask for the manufacturer's rough-opening dimensions and finished wall build-up. The measurements vary between systems and door sizes. If the work means making a wall thicker, show the resulting room dimensions on the plan. The improvement in circulation should still make sense after that change.

Plan switches and wiring early. Eclisse's wiring-ready pocket system includes a dedicated wiring channel. Its existence is useful evidence that this detail needs a designed solution; it does not mean wiring can be added anywhere in an ordinary pocket wall. Have the installer and electrician coordinate the actual specification.

Make the closed door part of the room

A pocket door has two appearances. Open, it is mostly an opening. Closed, it is a large vertical surface. Choose a finish you like in both states, especially where the door sits opposite a sofa or dining table.

Timber can give a plain partition warmth, but compare the leaf with the floor and nearby joinery. They do not need identical grain. A quieter relationship between two timbers often feels easier than an almost-match. A painted leaf can settle into the wall, with the frame and skirting doing more of the visual work.

Flush detailing needs careful coordination at the opening, ceiling and floor. A conventional architrave is not automatically a lesser choice. In an older house, it may connect the new door to existing joinery more comfortably than an isolated frameless opening.

Try the handle before committing

A recessed pull can look beautifully discreet and still be awkward to use. Test whether you can grasp it comfortably, move the leaf without scraping your fingers and retrieve the door when it is fully open. The edge pull matters just as much as the face fitting.

Think about everyone who will use the room, including visitors. A system that needs a small precise movement may be frustrating for someone with limited grip. Ask the supplier to demonstrate the proposed hardware rather than deciding from a close-up photograph.

Soft closing can make the last part of the movement gentler, but compatibility depends on the door and system. Check leaf weight, fitting requirements and how it will be adjusted. The finished door should move predictably without needing a special technique.

Be honest about sound and privacy

A sliding leaf does not automatically provide the same separation as a well-sealed hinged door. Gaps, seals, the door construction and the surrounding partition affect sound transmission. If the room will be used for calls or sleeping, ask for relevant performance information for the complete assembly.

Bathroom and bedroom doors need a comfortable privacy arrangement. Check the lock, emergency-release provision where appropriate and the way the leading edge meets the receiving jamb. Glass adds another question: what remains visible when the room behind is lit after dark?

Fire, access and escape requirements depend on the building and the door's location. Have the designer confirm what is needed before ordering. A standard pocket kit and a separately purchased leaf should not be assumed to form a suitable rated assembly.

Keep the pocket wall useful without damaging it

Decide what will go on the wall beside the opening. Shelving, pictures, switches and a television may all need fixings or services where the leaf travels. Ask the supplier what can be attached, where and with which fixings. A screw extending into the cavity can interfere with the door.

Leave space for everyday cleaning at the bottom guide and around the opening. Ask how the running gear can be accessed later and whether trim needs to be removable. A disappearing door is less appealing if a small adjustment requires damage to freshly finished plaster.

Eclisse's assembly library separates instructions by system and accessory. Use the exact instructions for the selected product, and keep them with the house records. A visually similar kit may have different installation and maintenance details.

Compare the simpler options on the same plan

Sometimes rehanging a hinged door solves the collision. A surface-mounted sliding door is another option, though it occupies wall face space and has its own privacy and fixing requirements. Compare the finished layouts and work involved rather than choosing from isolated door photographs.

If you only need to soften a view between two areas, a timber slat divider may suit the brief. It will not close the room or stop conversation. If daylight is the priority while retaining a fixed wall, consider an internal window.

The best pocket-door idea is usually quite specific: a clear route past a desk, a dining room that opens for friends, or a pantry door that no longer meets the fridge. Name that improvement before specifying the hardware. It keeps the design anchored in a room you can actually use.

Pocket door questions

Are pocket doors good for small rooms?

They can be useful where a door swing causes a real layout conflict. The wall must have enough suitable space for the chosen pocket system.

Can an existing door become a pocket door?

Sometimes, but the surrounding wall, services, opening and leaf compatibility need assessment. It is usually more involved than replacing hinges.

Can you hang shelves on a pocket-door wall?

Only as permitted by the specified system and fixing design. Check before drilling into the area where the leaf travels.

title: A Timber Slat Screen Can Give One Room Two Places to Be
seo: Timber Slat Room Divider Ideas for Small Open-Plan Homes
description: Explore timber slat room divider ideas for entrances, desks and living rooms, with advice on spacing, light, privacy, finishes and practical fixing details.
deck: A little separation can make an open room easier to live in. The gaps are as important as the timber.
alt: Fixed oak slat room divider separating a small entrance bench from a linen sofa
inline_sources: Writing desk and chair seen through an open oak slat screen beside a living room
Oak battens meeting a matching bottom rail with open gaps between them
body:
A timber slat room divider can mark out an entrance, desk area or dining corner while keeping views and some daylight moving through an open room. It provides partial visual separation rather than a closed private space. The useful design decisions are where the screen begins and ends, how it affects the route through the room, and what you can see through it from different angles.

Open-plan rooms can have a small domestic problem: everything arrives at once. You open the front door and see the sofa, the desk, the washing on a chair and somebody's abandoned shoes. A short screen can slow that view down. The room remains connected, but the entrance has somewhere to land.

The short answer

Give the screen one clear job

Choose the view or boundary you want to change, then mark the screen's position with tape. Test a full-size sample of the slats and gaps from several angles. Keep the walking route clear and have the supports, fixings and any safety requirements designed for the actual location.

Use a short screen to make an entrance feel separate

An entrance screen works well when it gives the first few steps into the house a little definition. It might sit beside a bench or between the front door and the end of the sofa. The aim is to create a useful arrival area, with enough room to take off a coat without standing in the living space.

Begin with the shoes, bags and door swing. A beautiful partition is unhelpful if the bench becomes difficult to reach or the front door hits its rail. Mark the proposed screen on the floor and walk through with a shopping bag in each hand. The route often tells you to make it shorter.

Keep storage on the drawing too. Battens are not automatically a sensible place for hooks or shelves. A solid wall nearby can do that work more quietly, leaving the screen as a simple boundary. Our small entryway guide has more ideas for making the arrival area useful.

A screened desk still belongs to the same room

Slats can soften the sight of a work surface from the sofa. Place the screen where it conceals the part of the desk that bothers you, rather than automatically enclosing the whole area. Sometimes hiding the monitor's back and the cable route is enough.

Allow for the chair when someone is sitting in it and when they get up. Check the view from the desk as well. A screen that looks airy from the living room may feel surprisingly dense when you sit close to it for several hours.

The gaps will not keep conversation or work calls contained. If quiet is a priority, you may need a closed room with an appropriate door and partition instead. A pocket door is one possible layout discussion where there is enough suitable wall space.

Test the gaps at full size

There is no single spacing that suits every home. Slat depth, width and the distance between them work together. Straight on, you may see plenty of the next area. From an oblique angle, the same screen can read as an almost continuous timber surface.

Make a sample with several battens in the proposed sizes and finish. Place it where the screen will stand, then look from the entrance, the sofa and the dining chair. A small material swatch cannot show this changing relationship between solid and open space.

Test privacy after dark with the lights on. The room beyond may become much more visible when it is brighter than your side. If you want to conceal a desk or seating area completely, an open slat screen is unlikely to meet the brief on its own.

Keep the useful daylight route open

An open screen still places timber in the path of light. Before positioning it between a window and the back of the room, check what that means for the darker area. More gaps may help the view feel lighter, but the result also depends on the screen's depth and angle.

Look at the room on a cloudy day as well as when sunlight draws attractive stripes across the floor. Those shadows can be lovely, but they are a brief part of the room's life. The bench behind the screen should remain pleasant when the sun is elsewhere.

If the main goal is to bring daylight into an enclosed space, start with the source of that light. An internal window can share light from an adjoining room while retaining a glazed division. In a single-storey extension, a well-positioned rooflight addresses a different part of the plan.

Choose timber for the whole room

Oak is an easy starting point, but the finish needs to sit comfortably with the floor, doors and furniture. Take the sample into the room rather than selecting it under showroom lighting. An orange cast that is barely noticeable on one small piece becomes more obvious across repeated battens.

Ask whether the proposed product is solid timber, veneered material or another construction, and how its edges and ends are finished. These details affect both its appearance and the way it should be specified. Armstrong's WoodWorks partition data, for example, includes both solid-wood and veneered options. It illustrates why a timber appearance alone does not tell you the material build-up.

A painted screen can work when the house already has painted joinery. Test the surface for cleaning and fingerprints, especially beside an entrance. A high-contrast dark finish may make the gaps look stronger; a quieter colour can let the screen sit further into the background.

Resolve the top and bottom before ordering the battens

Decide how the screen meets the floor and ceiling. Continuous rails can give the repetition a clear beginning and end. Other details may suit a more minimal room, but the fixing still needs to work. Ask the joiner to show how each piece is held and how the finished assembly resists movement.

Ceilings and floors are not always level. A measured survey helps avoid a line of uneven gaps or improvised packing at the top. If there is underfloor heating or concealed wiring, establish safe fixing positions before drilling. The proposed supports need to suit the building, not merely the appearance of a reference image.

Think about cleaning between the battens and around the bottom rail. Try your usual vacuum attachment against the sample. In a kitchen-adjacent position, consider how the finish will cope with the way you clean and use that part of the room.

Keep decorative screening separate from safety barriers

A room divider beside a level living area has a different job from guarding a stair or raised floor edge. Do not assume a decorative slat kit is suitable as a barrier. Where falls, escape routes or other safety requirements are involved, have the entire design assessed for that role.

The same applies to claims about sound. Timber slats sold as a decorative screen are not automatically an acoustic partition. If a supplier gives performance information, check what construction was tested and whether it matches the proposed installation.

Stop when the boundary is doing enough. Repeating the same slats on the television wall, ceiling and hallway can make a small room feel busy. A single short run, with a plain wall and everyday furniture around it, often gives the eye more room to rest.

Timber room divider questions

How far apart should room-divider slats be?

Choose the spacing with the slat width and depth, then test a full-size sample from the room's main viewpoints. There is no universal decorative spacing, and safety-related locations require a separate assessment.

Do slat dividers provide privacy?

They provide partial visual screening. Views change with angle and lighting, and sound travels through the gaps.

Can a slat screen make a small room feel smaller?

Yes, particularly if it blocks a useful route or the main daylight source. Try a shorter run and test the layout before committing.

Sources and image note

The material example was checked against Armstrong's product data linked above; that commercial system is not a specification for the fictional domestic scenes. Layout and styling advice is by.foro editorial analysis. Images are AI-generated architectural visualisations.
